question.text: In many situations, to find the electric field using the gauss law, we can use the simplified equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced close="|" open="|"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>enclosed</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mfenced close="|" open="|"><mover><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math> is the permittivity of free space, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math> is the area of Gaussian surface and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>enclosed</mi></msub></math> is the net charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface. Among the following situations, this equation can be used

options.text: only when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface
only when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mfenced></math> is constant on the surface

only when the Gaussian surface is an equipotential surface and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mfenced></math> is constant of the surface
for any choice of Gaussian surface

solution.text: Magnitude of electric field is constant $\&$ the surface is equipotential
